questions.q: Huguenot settlers planted vines at New Paltz in 1677 in the valley of which river, now one of the Court's Certified New York AVAs?
questions.exp: The Hudson River Region AVA of 1982 follows the tidal Hudson north of New York City, where the river tempers a hard continental winter; Brotherhood Winery at Washingtonville, founded in 1839, is counted the oldest continuously operating winery in the United States. The Court's other two Certified AVAs are Lake Erie in the far west and Long Island in the Atlantic.

questions.q: Most of the Concord grown along the lake shore in New York's Lake Erie AVA never becomes wine. What is the bulk of that crop grown for?
questions.exp: The Lake Erie shore is a grape belt planted overwhelmingly to Concord, and most of the crop is sold to processors for grape juice and jelly rather than fermented; the lake holds back budburst until the spring frosts have passed and stretches the autumn. The Finger Lakes, the Court's Introductory AVA, carry New York's fine wine reputation instead.

questions.q: Which climate category does the Court give New York State, moderated by its lakes, rivers and ocean?
questions.exp: New York is continental, with cold winters that can kill vinifera buds and trunks, so the vineyards gather where water softens the extremes: the deep Finger Lakes and Lake Erie inland, the Hudson in its valley, and the Atlantic around Long Island. The water stores summer heat into autumn and holds bud break back in spring.

questions.q: What carved the long, deep troughs that hold the Finger Lakes?
opts: A rift in the earth's crust
questions.exp: Ice-age glaciers gouged the Finger Lakes out of old river valleys, leaving narrow troughs so deep, Seneca above all, that they rarely freeze and give back stored summer heat through the winter. That is the Court's physical feature: deep glacial lakes that keep the slopes above them alive through cold that kills vines a few miles inland.

questions.q: Besides deep winter freezes, which summer threat does the Court say New York growers must guard their vines against?
questions.exp: Humid eastern summers with rain through the season bring downy and powdery mildew and botrytis, so New York growers spray, open the canopy to the breeze and choose resistant grapes; the hybrids were bred partly for that resistance. The winter half of the Court's cell is the cold, which the lakes and the ocean blunt.

questions.q: Which aromatic white, scented of lychee and rose, does the Court list for New York beside Riesling and Chardonnay?
questions.exp: Gewürztraminer is a Finger Lakes speciality beside Riesling, made dry to off dry with its lychee, rose and spice kept vivid by the cool lake climate. The Court's Introductory whites for New York are Riesling, Gewürztraminer and Chardonnay, with the hybrids Aurore and Seyval Blanc added at the Certified level.

questions.q: Aurore, once widely planted in the Finger Lakes for sparkling and blended wine, belongs to which family of vine?
questions.exp: Aurore, also known as Seibel 5279, is a white French-American hybrid bred in France by the hybridiser Albert Seibel to join vinifera's flavour to American hardiness and disease resistance; early ripening, it was long a workhorse of New York's sparkling and blended wines. Seyval Blanc, the Court's other named hybrid, is the crisper grape still widely grown.

questions.q: Which red vinifera on the Court's New York list survives a Finger Lakes winter better than Merlot and ripens where Cabernet Sauvignon struggles?
questions.exp: Cabernet Franc ripens a week or so before Cabernet Sauvignon and has hardier wood, so it is the eastern red that works both by the Finger Lakes and on Long Island, fragrant and leafy with bright acid. Merlot succeeds in Long Island's long maritime autumn but struggles by the lakes; the Court's red list is Pinot Noir, Merlot and Cabernet Franc.

questions.q: Besides Merlot and Cabernet Franc, which red grape does the Court list for New York, grown by the cooler lakes for light reds and sparkling base?
questions.exp: Pinot Noir, early ripening and at home in cool climates, gives light, red fruited reds and the base of traditional method sparkling wine in the Finger Lakes. Zinfandel, Grenache and Malbec need far more heat and a longer season than a New York summer offers.

questions.q: Tasters have a one-word name for the pungent, musky aroma that marks Concord and other Vitis labrusca grapes. What is it?
questions.exp: Foxy is the trade's word for the grapey, musky, candied scent of Concord, Catawba and Niagara, the labrusca grapes native to North America; methyl anthranilate carries much of it. Most of New York's Concord, the Court's Certified red, goes to juice and jelly along Lake Erie rather than into dry wine.

questions.q: Dr Konstantin Frank proved vinifera could survive in the Finger Lakes and opened his own winery in 1962. On the shore of which lake?
questions.exp: Frank, a Ukrainian-born émigré hired by Gold Seal in 1953, argued that vinifera had failed in the east from the wrong roots rather than the cold, grafted Riesling and Chardonnay onto hardy rootstock, and in 1962 opened Vinifera Wine Cellars on Keuka Lake near Hammondsport. The state's vinifera industry descends from that proof.
